newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD French short term economic outlook-full text.
newsitem.headline: OECD French short term economic outlook-full text.

text.p: The following is the full text of a chapter in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development's February 1997 economic survey of France.

Recent indicators point to the continuation of slow growth for the remainder of 1996. Business confidence and domestic and export order books have started to recover but are still at a relatively low level. Consumer confidence has also remained low. However, consumption of durables rose strongly in the third quarter of 1996, prior to the expiration of incentives to buy new cars; a considerable decline in the fourth quarter is expected. On the other hand, the recovery in the housing market could solidify over the next few months. While the strong investment growth predicted in business surveys for 1996 should probably be discounted, a modest rise in business investment in the second half of 1996 is projected.

The OECD's fiscal projections are based on the measures announced in the 1996 and 1997 budgets and incorporate the measures affecting the social security schemes described below. It is assumed that social spending growth will be somewhat above the official projections. For 1998, no further tax cuts or reductions in employer's social security contribution rates are included. Overall, the fiscal stance between 1996 and 1998 embodied in this scenario is mildly restrictive. Long-term interest rates are expected to continue to follow German rates and rise somewhat over the projection period. Short-term rates could ease back further over the next few months but rise thereafter, with some further decline in the differential against German rates.

The current economic weakness should dissipate progressively and output growth may accelerate to 2-1/2 percent in 1997 and 1998. Business investment is expected to rebound due to reasonable profitability, the gradual take-up of spare capacity, and the more favourable outlook for demand. Lower interest rates and government incentives should lead to stronger growth of residential construction. Better employment prospects and faster income gains should bolster consumer spending. Stockbuilding could rise from the low levels of early 1996, and its contribution to growth could be substantial over the projection period. The international environment is set to improve, with export markets projected to grow by six to seven percent throughout the forecast period, with the current account surplus rising somewhat further. Employment growth is expected to increase, and the unemployment rate could be 12 percent by the end of 1998. Wage inflation is likely to remain low given the amount of cyclical slack in the labour m

The projections point to a revival in economic activity, largely due to stronger foreign demand and much easier monetary conditions. However, there is considerable range of uncertainty about the interest rate sensitivity of the French economy. Earlier empirical work did not show significant effects on growth from interest rate changes. However, more recent research provides evidence that such effects could have risen markedly since the financial market liberalisation in the mid-1980s. In addition, monetary easing in France came later than in many other European economies, but was stronger in the first half of 1996. This could imply a more hesitant recovery than elsewhere, but stronger growth later on. The substantial destocking in the first half of 1996 could lead to a more pronounced stock cycle than projected. On the other hand, the saving ratio has fallen considerably and a rebound above the baseline projection cannot be excluded -- at least in the short run.
